summary: The paper has no welfare, willingness-to-pay or causal effect-size claims, so the magnitude remit is narrow. It covers headline agreement, yield and count statistics, a cost claim, descriptive listing shares and proposed-design interpretation. I found ten places where magnitude language changes interpretation: (1) the 97% agreement figure has no prevalence baseline, (2) date agreement rests on three articles about two projects, (3) the headline counts of 92 articles, 43 projects and 29 dated projects have no error rates, (4) "day or month" dating is presented as success although exact timing is the stated need, (5) the pilot yield mixes events and articles, (6) the seasonal clustering claim reports no figures, (7) the county ranking reports no counts, (8) "cheap" has no comparator, (9) the listing-mention inference has no baseline or minimum meaningful change, and (10) the ceremony/date-precision gap is read as an attention effect. I read the main text, tables and appendix from the page text and did not use the flagged structured table CSV/markdown. Parser fallbacks were sufficient.

findings.finding_summary: The 97% human–LLM relevance agreement is presented as evidence of near-human performance without a prevalence baseline. Only 3 of 34 pilot articles are relevant and about 3% of the full run is relevant, so a trivial all-'not relevant' rule would score about 91% in the pilot and about 97% in the full run.

location.text_quote: Table 4 shows that the pilot coder and the LLM agree on 97 percent of the articles

findings.claim_text: The LLM agrees with the pilot coder on relevance for 97 percent of articles, the same as between two human coders, indicating comparable performance.
findings.evidence_summary: Table 4 shows 33 of 34 correct, but the pilot coder labels 31 articles not relevant and 3 relevant. An all-negative classifier would therefore match the pilot coder on 31/34 ≈ 91%. In the full run only 92 of 3,187 articles (≈2.9%) are relevant, so overall agreement is then nearly uninformative. The LLM flagged 4 articles as relevant and 3 matched the pilot coder (precision 3/4); recall is 3/3 on three positives. The paper does note the sample is small and results are indicative only. It does not report positive-class precision/recall, kappa or any chance-corrected measure. The 'same as human–human' comparison has the same baseline problem, because Table 3 also has 30 true negatives.

findings.finding_summary: The claim that the LLM gives the same opening date as the pilot coder 'in all three' relevant articles (versus two of three for the humans) rests on three articles about only two projects, with no tolerance or precision definition. The comparison should not be read as showing better date accuracy.

location.text_quote: The LLM gives the same date as the pilot coder in all three.

findings.claim_text: The LLM gives the same opening date as the pilot coder for all three relevant articles, whereas the two human coders agree on two of three.
findings.evidence_summary: Section 3.1.4 says that of the five relevant articles only two unique openings were found. Four articles mention Homborsund and one Stod. Two Homborsund articles are recoded not relevant, which leaves three articles: two on Homborsund and one on Stod. Date agreement is thus tested on two independent events, and 3/3 vs 2/3 is within sampling noise. The human disagreement was a definitional choice (official opening vs start of school year), and the LLM matched the pilot coder's definition. The abstract and introduction repeat 'same opening date for all three relevant articles' without noting the n=3, two-project basis. The paper warns generally that results are indicative, but no date-accuracy rate with an interval is given for the pipeline.

findings.finding_summary: The headline results (92 articles reporting an opening, 43 projects, 14 of 15 counties, 29 dated) are presented as discoveries without false-positive or false-negative rates. The pilot suggests precision of only 3/4, and the grouping of 92 articles into 43 projects is unvalidated.

location.text_quote: The result was 92 articles reporting an opening and 43 unique

findings.claim_text: Applied to 3,187 articles, the pipeline finds 92 articles reporting an opening, grouped into 43 projects across 14 of 15 counties.
findings.evidence_summary: No full-run validation is reported; Section 8 says a random sample should still be checked against human coding. In the pilot the LLM flagged 4 articles relevant (Table 4) and one was a false positive (the Stord article), so precision was 3/4 on a tiny base. If anything like that held in the full run, a material share of the 92 would not be openings. Recall is unknown, so the counts are neither a lower nor an upper bound, and no benchmark exists for how many openings occurred in the period. Project grouping was done by hand and is not validated. Counts such as '14 of 15 counties' and '29 dated' then inherit this uncertainty. The conclusion that the pipeline 'identifies 43 unique projects' reads as a result rather than an unvalidated yield.

findings.finding_summary: The abstract, introduction and conclusion highlight '29 of them dated to the day or month' as success, but the paper's own motivation requires exact opening dates. Only 19 of 43 projects (≈44%) are day-precise, and month-only dates cannot place listings before or after an opening within that month.

location.text_quote: 29 of them dated to the day or month

findings.claim_text: The pipeline groups openings into 43 projects, 29 of which are dated to the day or month.
findings.evidence_summary: Table 6 gives Day 19, Month 10, Year 9, Not stated 5 (sum 43). The introduction says before-after designs depend on knowing exactly when each route opened, and Section 6.3 says imprecise dating can bias a difference-in-differences toward zero and that model (2) may need to be limited to precisely dated projects. Day-precise projects are 19/43 ≈ 44%, versus 29/43 ≈ 67% in the headline. Month-level dates would leave the opening month ambiguous in a monthly design. Neither the abstract nor the conclusion qualifies this, and date correctness itself is not validated for the full run.

findings.claim_text: Only 2 of the 34 unique articles (about 6 percent) concern an opening that took place, so keyword search alone is too noisy.
findings.evidence_summary: Section 3.1.4 states that of five relevant articles, only two unique openings were found (four articles on Homborsund, one on Stod). Figure 1's funnel itself shows 'Coded relevant 5' before 'Distinct openings that took place 2'. The article-level share concerning an actual opening is therefore 5/34 ≈ 15% (the Figure 1 '15 % retained'), or 3/34 ≈ 9% after the two pre-opening articles are recoded not relevant. The Figure 1 caption also gives 'Only 2 of 70 search hits', mixing events with hits that include duplicates. The qualitative conclusion that yield is low remains, but the stated percentage understates the article-level yield. The 6% compares events with articles. The abstract's 'only two actual openings' is a correct event count.

findings.finding_summary: The claim that 'openings cluster before winter and summer holidays' is drawn from a ranking of the share of relevant articles by period, with no shares, counts or denominators reported. The unit is articles, not openings, and the archive has few July–August articles.

location.text_quote: This indicates that openings cluster before winter and summer

findings.claim_text: October–December 2025 and May–June 2026 have the highest share of relevant articles, which indicates that openings cluster before winter and summer holidays.
findings.evidence_summary: The paper reports no period-specific numbers; only the ordering of periods is given. The share of relevant articles is a ratio of articles flagged relevant to all articles retrieved. It depends on search volume and on how many articles describe one opening (up to four for Homborsund). It is not a count or share of openings, and with 43 projects, small monthly or quarterly counts make the ranking fragile. The text itself notes the July–August extraction is thin, so the stated pre-summer peak cannot be judged against the summer months.

findings.finding_summary: The proposal to read any rise in any type of cycling mention near a new route as evidence that the route made cycling 'a stronger selling point' lacks a baseline and a magnitude interpretation. Cycling is mentioned in 38% of listings, the share rose about 9 percentage points over the period, and county shares range from about 7% to 61%.

location.section: 6.1 An application to house listing data
location.text_quote: and storage. An increase in any type of mention would thus indicate that the route has made

findings.claim_text: An increase in any type of cycling mention in listings would indicate that the route has made cycling a stronger selling point.
findings.evidence_summary: The appendix shows high and heterogeneous base rates. Cycling is mentioned in 38.1% of listings overall, rising from about 35% in 2020 to about 44% at the end of the period, and ranging from 60.8% in Oslo to 6.8% in Møre og Romsdal. Mentions pool infrastructure, parking/storage, proximity and generic 'sykkel' words, and the paper calls the keyword classification coarse. The paper does not say what size of change would be economically or informationally meaningful. A mention-share change for a local route is also not mapped to house-price capitalisation, which is the motivating comparison with Gibbons and Machin (2005). The hypotheses θ>0 and δ>0 are sign-only. The design uses project-by-month fixed effects, which could absorb the secular trend, but no expected effect size or power consideration is given. This is a proposal, not an estimated result.

findings.finding_summary: The contrast between 17 of 18 projects with a ceremony dated to the day and 2 of 26 without is read as showing that date precision 'depends on how much attention an opening receives'. A reported ceremony is also a mechanical source of an explicit date, and the raw gap is not a measure of attention.

location.text_quote: This suggests that the precision of the dates is not random but

findings.claim_text: Of 44 projects, 17 of 18 with a reported ceremony are dated to the day versus 2 of 26 without, suggesting date precision depends on attention.
findings.evidence_summary: 17/18 ≈ 94% versus 2/26 ≈ 8% is a very large raw gap. The paper reads it as an attention effect, but a ceremony article typically reports the date of the event, so ceremony and day-precise date may be linked by construction rather than through attention. Project size, project type and coverage depth are not held constant here. The paper goes on to propose an ordered model (1) to test this, so the sentence is hypothesis-generating. The word 'suggests' hedges it only partly.

notes: No welfare, willingness-to-pay or causal effect-size estimates are reported; those checks are not applicable.

Parser-quality guidance was followed. All quotes come from pages/page_NNN.md. The structured table CSV/markdown and the Figure 1 crop were not used, and Figure 1 chart values were read from page-4 text only.
Table 8 and Figure 2/4 shares were read from the page text. Listing counts such as 266 625 / 700 579 = 38.1% are consistent and were not raised as magnitude issues.
External literature magnitudes (for example the Fosgerau et al. 60 percent and the Fyhri et al. five percentage points) were not verified against the cited papers and were not raised as findings.

coverage.reason: Ten magnitude-interpretation issues were found (MAG-001 to MAG-010). No welfare, WTP or calibration claims exist in the paper, so those checks are not applicable. The main text and appendix were read in full, but the external citations' magnitudes were not verified.
